hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers, including Flock cameras, from state highways within 30 days. The department cited concerns over rapid expansion, data privacy, misuse and surveillance schemes in announcing the directive.

The announcement follows public statements by Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the technology out of control days earlier and raised concerns about Florida becoming a surveillance state. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records. The decision affects cameras operated by local law enforcement agencies and municipalities that have installed the devices on state-controlled roadways.

Palm Beach County residents expressed divided opinions on the order. Reid Mollway said the level of data collection represents an invasion of privacy, noting that tracking data is not fully clarified and is kept for dates that have no expiration. David Vega and other residents defended the cameras as serving an important public safety purpose. Vega said the cameras allow people to walk streets and use highways more safely.

Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw provided a statement to WPTV, though the content was not detailed in the report. Multiple local law enforcement agencies have been contacted for comment but have not yet responded to the state order.

hero.body:
The Florida Department of Transportation is ordering local agencies to remove automated license plate readers from state highways within 30 days, citing concerns over rapid expansion, data privacy, misuse and surveillance schemes. The order affects cameras including Flock brand readers that local police agencies use as surveillance and public safety tools. More than 8,000 Flock cameras are documented across Florida, according to state records.

The announcement comes days after Gov. Ron DeSantis publicly called the technology "out of control" and raised concerns about Florida becoming a surveillance state. The decision is drawing mixed reactions from Palm Beach County residents. Reid Mollway, a Palm Beach County resident who supports the move, said the level of data collection is an invasion of privacy. "We're being tracked through data that is not fully clarified and kept for dates that have no expiration," Mollway said.

David Vega, another Palm Beach County resident, said the cameras serve an important public safety purpose. "I support them being there," Vega said. Vega and others argue the cameras help law enforcement keep communities safer. "It is something that allows us to walk our street and be on the highways more safely," another resident said.

The crackdown is also drawing political criticism. Nikki Fried, chair of the Florida Democratic Party, criticized Republicans for allowing the unchecked spread of the technology across the state. Palm Beach County Sheriff Ric Bradshaw sent WPTV a statement in response to the order.

hero.body:
A body was recovered from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge in Martin County on Tuesday morning, and investigators believe it is Michael Anthony Debevec, a Port St. Lucie man reported missing in late August. Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said the body has not been officially identified, but the deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing when he disappeared.

The search began Saturday when a Good Samaritan found a wallet belonging to Debevec and went to his home to return it, prompting his family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered. The discoveries prompted detectives and ground and aerial units to launch an extensive search of the area.

Investigators determined that Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. on August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. Phone records showed that his phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge. On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body.

Budensiek said investigators had not officially confirmed whether the body was Debevec's. He said there was a lot of decomposition that had taken place, making it impossible to determine cause of death. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found. The sheriff said the investigation is ongoing.

hero.body:
A body was recovered Tuesday from deep within the mangroves near the House of Refuge on Hutchinson Island, and Martin County Sheriff John Budensiek said investigators believe it is Michael Anthony Debevec, a Port St. Lucie man reported missing last week. The deceased person was wearing clothing matching what Debevec was believed to have been wearing, but decomposition prevented officials from officially confirming the identity or determining a cause of death. The discovery followed an extensive search prompted by a Good Samaritan finding Debevec's wallet Saturday and trying to return it.

Budensiek laid out the search timeline at a news conference Tuesday. The Good Samaritan went to Debevec's home to return the wallet, which led the family to file a missing person report. Investigators found Debevec's vehicle Saturday afternoon at Chastain Beach, a little more than two miles from where the body was discovered. Phone records showed Debevec traveled from the Port St. Lucie area to Martin County at about 3 a.m. August 27 and parked at Chastain Beach. His phone was in use Friday morning and moving back and forth between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge.

On Tuesday morning, investigators found a backpack belonging to Debevec hanging high in a tree with his computer inside. A deeper search into the mangroves led investigators to the body. Budensiek said the level of decomposition made it impossible to determine what happened. "So we do believe we found Mr. Debevec. Unfortunately, there's a lot of decomposition that's taken place so it's really impossible to determine cause of death. What are we dealing with here? I don't know," Budensiek said.

The discovery marks an unexplained death in a heavily visited public shoreline area along Hutchinson Island. Debevec's family was notified that a body was found. The investigation involved detectives and ground and aerial units conducting an extensive search of the area between Chastain Beach and the House of Refuge.
